cover.artAlt: A deep-sea submersible with bright headlights shining out into dark blue water
cover.blurb: Most of the ocean is deeper than sunlight can reach. Switch on the lights and come down.

pages.title: Animals That Make Their Own Light
pages.artAlt: A glowing translucent jellyfish drifting in pitch-black water

facts.text: Bioluminescence is light made by a living thing, using a chemical reaction inside its own body. It is cold light, so it never burns, and far down in the sea it is often the only light there is.

About 80 out of every 100 animals living between about 660 and 3,300 feet down can make their own light. Jellyfish, squid and fish all glow, and scientists are still working out everything they use their light for.
facts.artAlt: A glowing deep-sea squid hanging upright in black water, lines of blue-green light running along its body and arms
facts.caption: A squid switches on its own blue-green light in the dark.

facts.text: The ocean comes in layers. The top 660 feet is the sunlight zone. From 660 feet down to 3,300 feet is the twilight zone, dim and blue. Below 3,300 feet is the midnight zone, where no sunlight reaches at all.
facts.artAlt: Looking up from deep underwater, pale shafts of sunlight fade from bright blue near the surface into darkness below
facts.caption: Looking up from the twilight zone, the sunlight is nearly gone.

infographic.title: How far down do the ocean's layers go?

rows.label: The Statue of Liberty, ground to torch
The bottom of the sunlight zone
The bottom of the twilight zone
The bottom of the midnight zone

infographic.caption: The three layer depths come from NOAA. The Statue of Liberty is 305 feet from the ground to her torch, and she is here only so you have something to measure against. Almost every glowing animal lives in the middle band.

pages.title: Hot Springs on the Sea Floor
pages.artAlt: Hydrothermal vents on the sea floor puffing out black smoke, with pale tube worms growing around them

facts.text: In some places on the sea floor, seawater sinks into cracks near undersea volcanoes, gets heated deep inside the Earth, and shoots straight back out. Scientists have measured that water at about 750 degrees Fahrenheit, more than three times hotter than boiling water.

The dark plumes are nicknamed black smokers, but that is not smoke. The hot water is packed with dissolved minerals, and when it meets the near-freezing seawater those minerals turn solid in a swirling dark cloud and slowly stack up into rocky chimneys.
facts.artAlt: A close view of a black smoker vent, a thick dark plume of mineral-filled water gushing out of the top of a craggy rock chimney
facts.caption: That dark cloud is not smoke. It is minerals turning solid in the cold.

facts.text: Nothing down here has sunlight to live on, so life runs on chemicals instead. Tiny microbes turn vent chemicals into food, a trick called chemosynthesis. The big pale tube worms have no mouth and no stomach at all, because microbes living inside them do the feeding.
facts.artAlt: A close view of a bunch of tube worms, tall pale tubes with bright red feathery tips, packed together on the rock beside a vent
facts.caption: Tube worms crowd around a vent, red tips waving in the water.

infographic.title: How hot is the water coming out?

rows.label: Water shooting out of a vent

infographic.caption: The vent temperature comes from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The bath, the pot and the oven are everyday temperatures, here only so you have something to measure against. Every number is in degrees Fahrenheit.

pages.title: The Whale That Dives Deepest
pages.artAlt: A sperm whale swimming downward into deep blue water

facts.text: A sperm whale looks for its food by diving. It goes down to around 2,000 feet again and again, and one dive can last about 45 minutes, all on the single breath it took at the surface.

Down that deep it is pitch black, so the whale sees with sound. It makes loud clicks and listens for the echoes coming back. The closer it gets to a squid, the faster the clicks come, until they run together into a sound scientists call a buzz.
facts.artAlt: A sperm whale hanging head down in deep blue water, its huge square head pointing into the dark below
facts.caption: Head down in the dark, the whale listens for its own echoes.

facts.text: A male sperm whale can grow to about 52 feet, longer than a school bus. Much of that enormous square head is a sac of waxy oil called spermaceti, which helps the whale aim its clicks into the dark.
facts.artAlt: A whole sperm whale seen from the side in open blue water, blunt square head at one end, wrinkled gray body and wide tail at the other
facts.caption: From square head to tail, a big male is longer than a school bus.

infographic.title: How long is a sperm whale?
infographic.caption: The whale's length comes from NOAA Fisheries. The kid and the school bus are everyday sizes, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: The Bottom of the Deep
pages.artAlt: The dark sea floor of pale sand with a sea star and a small pale octopus lit by a submersible lamp

facts.text: Below about 660 feet the ocean turns cold and heavy. Down deep the average temperature is around 39 degrees Fahrenheit, close to the inside of a fridge, and the water presses down hundreds of times harder than the air does at the beach.

Animals really do live on the soft muddy bottom: sea stars, sea cucumbers and pale deep-sea octopuses. Researchers watch them using robot submarines that carry their own lights and cameras, because otherwise there is nothing to see by.
facts.artAlt: A pale deep-sea octopus and a bright red sea star sitting on soft gray mud, lit by the lamps of a robot submarine
facts.caption: A robot submarine's lamps light up one small patch of the muddy bottom.

facts.text: We have barely looked. By 2026 about 29 percent of the world's sea floor had been mapped in detail, and explorers have actually laid eyes on less than one thousandth of one percent of the deep sea floor, an area about the size of Rhode Island.
facts.artAlt: A screen on a research ship showing a colorful sonar map of ridges and valleys on the sea floor
facts.caption: Sound sent down from a ship draws a map of the bottom.

infographic.title: How we found out what the bottom looks like

stops.label: Ships lower a heavy weight on a very long rope, over and over, just to feel where the bottom is
Ships send sound down instead and listen for the echo, which draws a map. That is how about 29 percent of the sea floor has been mapped
Robot submarines swim down carrying their own lights, and even now less than one thousandth of one percent of the deep sea floor has been seen with our own eyes

infographic.caption: The mapping and exploring numbers come from NOAA Ocean Exploration. The steps show how the tools changed, not how long each one took.
